title: Scoring a model: which number matters
hook: Accuracy can lie when outcomes are rare. Choose the score by the cost of each mistake.
inPlainWords: There are two kinds of mistakes: a false alarm (flagged, but fine) and a miss (a real problem, not flagged). Which one hurts more decides the score you should watch.

useCase.title: A fraud alert on 100,000 payments
useCase.story: About 100 of them are fraud. False alarms annoy customers and cost review time. Misses cost real money.

approaches.name: Accuracy
approaches.what: The share of all answers that were right.
approaches.avoidWhen: Outcomes are rare. Saying "never fraud" scores 99.9%.

approaches.name: Precision
approaches.what: Of the payments we flagged, how many were truly fraud?

approaches.name: Recall
approaches.what: Of all the real fraud, how much did we flag?
approaches.avoidWhen: False alarms would flood the team.
approaches.example: Caught 30 of 100 frauds: three in ten.

approaches.name: A balance of both (F-score)
approaches.what: One number that drops if either precision or recall is poor.
approaches.greatWhen: You need a single number to compare models.
approaches.avoidWhen: The two mistakes have very different costs.

approaches.name: Cost in money
approaches.what: Put a price on each kind of mistake and add it up.
approaches.greatWhen: You know, or can estimate, the costs.
approaches.avoidWhen: You have no idea of the costs yet.
approaches.example: A miss costs $200 and a false alarm costs $3 in review time.

approaches.name: Choosing the threshold
approaches.what: Decide how sure the model must be before it flags something.
approaches.greatWhen: Any model that outputs a score.
approaches.example: Flag above 70% risk, or above 40% during holiday spikes.

challenge.question: Fraud is 0.1% of payments. A model that says "never fraud" is 99.9% accurate. What should lead your scoring?

options.why: It rewards the model for doing nothing.

options.text: Precision and recall, weighed by the cost of false alarms versus misses
options.why: It measures what actually matters: fraud caught, and customers annoyed.
You will catch fraud, but you could flag thousands of good customers.
A few obvious frauds get caught and the rest are missed.

bestCase.title: Price the mistakes, then tune the threshold
bestCase.example: A miss costs $200 and a false alarm costs $3, so the team accepts many false alarms to catch more fraud. They set the threshold to catch 8 in 10 frauds while keeping reviews manageable, and re-tune before holidays.

worstCase.title: Reporting accuracy on a rare event
worstCase.example: The dashboard shows 99.9% and the boss is thrilled. The model never flagged a single payment. Fraud losses keep growing for a whole quarter.

steps.label: Payment arrives
steps.goes: A new payment enters the system.

steps.label: Compare with the threshold
steps.goes: The threshold is 70%, so the payment is flagged.
steps.goesWrong: The threshold stays at a default that ignores the cost of misses, so this risky payment passes.

steps.label: Log the outcome
steps.goes: Confirmed fraud and false alarms are recorded.

steps.label: Re-tune monthly
steps.goes: Costs and the threshold are reviewed.

takeaway: Pick the score by the cost of each mistake, not because it looks good.
